Since they provide substantial structural members below sea-level, they were deemed by the authors of this report as the most suitable for the different methods of integration for housing or connecting to the OTEC equipment. Semi-submersibles therefore presented an opportunity to consider integrating an OTEC plant with a possibility of minimal disruption or need for change to the design. In the following sections, high level summaries of the considered integration approaches, including considerations, advantages, and disadvantages, are presented. 4.2.1 Small Hull-Integrated At the outset of this study, the authors were looking to hypothetically demonstrate how OTEC could be efficiently integrated as part of the design of the interior in one or more hull columns in a semi-submersible. This concept appeared to make sense since the hull can provide structural assurance to housing the OTEC equipment without significant added risk 2 Basd on actual facilities built as semi submersibles. However, hull integration also proved to be one of the primary limiting factors due to the limited space available in the hull’s interior without significant design modification. As discussed in the Objective 2 report, this leads to choices of comparatively small sized components, such as small diameter cold- and warm-water intake pipes and small condensers and evaporators. Based on the modeling of the OTEC plant, the integration of a small OTEC plant into a future hull column is possible with the configuration as presented in Table 3.
